note.text: To efficiently find the nexioms and the machine type: 1. Start by testing a group of 3 objects. 2. If it lights up, test a pair from that group. 3. If the pair lights up, test one of them individually. - If the individual lights up, the machine "needs one" and that object is a nexiom. Find the second nexiom among the remaining objects. - If the individual does not light up, test the other. If neither lights up individually but the pair does, the machine "needs two" and those are the nexioms. 4. If the initial group of 3 does not light up, you know the machine either "needs one" and both nexioms are in the other 3, or it "needs two" and at least one nexiom is in the other 3. Adjust your tests to narrow down the remaining candidates.

note.text: If you test half the objects (3) and it doesn't light up, and then test the other half (3) and it also doesn't light up, you immediately know the machine "needs two" and there is exactly one nexiom in each half. You can then find the nexioms by testing combinations across the two halves. For example, test one object from the first half together with all objects from the second half. If it lights up, that object is the first nexiom, and you can then test it individually with the objects from the second half to find the second nexiom.

note.text: If a group of 3 lights up, but a pair from it does not, the excluded object is definitely a nexiom. If that excluded object alone does not light up, you immediately know the machine "needs two" and the second nexiom is one of the objects in the tested pair. You can then test the excluded object with one of the objects from the pair. If it lights up, those two are the nexioms. If it doesn't, the excluded object and the other object from the pair are the nexioms. This efficiently identifies both the machine type and the nexioms within 4 tests.
